cuire_sans.intro: A frying pan isn't essential: embers, sticks and ashes are enough to cook fish, meat or bread.
etapes: Skewer: spear the food on a stick of sound dead wood, and hold it above the embers, not in the flame. Turn it often.
Flat fish: split it open, wedge it between two split sticks, and plant the whole thing at an angle facing the embers.
Ash bread: shape a thick flatbread (flour, water, salt), lay it on a very hot flat stone or wrap it around a stick above the embers.
Cooking under the ash: wrap potatoes, fish or vegetables in foil or large wet leaves, and bury them under the embers.
Hanging roast: hang a piece of meat in front of the fire on a wet string. As it dries, the string twists by itself and turns the meat.
attention: Never use yew, cherry laurel or holly wood for skewers: they're poisonous.
cuire_sans.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

trou_braises.intro: The old-timers' slow cooking: a pot buried in the embers cooks by itself while you sleep or walk.
etapes: Dig a hole a little bigger than your lidded pot (ideally cast iron).
Light a good fire in it and let it burn for an hour to heat the sides.
Remove some of the embers, put the closed pot at the bottom, put the embers back around and on top.
Cover with earth to keep the heat in.
Let it cook for 4 to 8 hours (beans, stew), then carefully clear away the earth.
attention: Only where fires are allowed, away from roots, and fill in the hole before leaving.
trou_braises.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

bannock.intro: The bread of the Far North voyageurs: a few dry ingredients, water, and a pan or a stick.
etapes: At home, mix in a bag: 2 glasses of flour, 1 teaspoon of baking powder, 1 pinch of salt, and if you like, powdered milk or sugar.
At camp, add water little by little until you get a soft dough that doesn't stick to your fingers.
In a pan: flatten the dough to 2 cm, cook over gentle embers, 8 to 10 minutes on each side.
On a stick: roll the dough into a long sausage, wind it in a spiral around a dry stick and hold it above the embers, turning it.
The bread is done when it sounds hollow when tapped.
bannock.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

lit_camp.intro: The cold that ruins a night almost always comes from the ground, not the air. A good bed insulates from below.
etapes: Never sleep directly on bare earth, even with a sleeping bag: the ground draws away your heat.
Choose flat, slightly raised ground, cleared of stones and branches.
With a mat: add a layer of dry dead leaves underneath to double the insulation.
Without a mat: pile up at least 20 to 30 cm of dry dead leaves, dry grass or dead bracken. Once compressed, a hand's thickness should remain.
Mark out the bed with two dead logs, one at the head and one at the feet, so the layer doesn't spread.
Lie down for a while, then add more padding where it has compressed.
attention: In Europe, you don't cut living trees or branches without the owner's permission: use dead wood fallen on the ground. The old-timers cut living fir boughs: today that is forbidden and unnecessary, as dead leaves insulate very well.
lit_camp.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

azimut_retour.titre: Retracing your steps with a compass
azimut_retour.intro: If you noted your direction when setting off, you can always come back: just follow the opposite direction.
etapes: When leaving the camp or path, take a bearing with the compass and note the angle (for example 60°).
To come back, add 180° if the angle is less than 180°, or subtract 180° otherwise (60° + 180° = 240°).
Set the compass to this new angle and walk aiming at successive landmarks: a tree, a rock, then the next one.
Check the compass every few minutes: you almost always drift to the same side without noticing.
If the sun or a shadow is suddenly on the “wrong” side, you've turned: stop and get back on track.
azimut_retour.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

perdu_calme.titre: Thinking you're lost: the right reflexes
perdu_calme.intro: Most accidents involving lost people come from panic, not the terrain. Your first tool is staying calm.
etapes: Stop, sit down, drink a little water. Don't set off again at random.
Remember the last safe place you recognise, and how long you've been walking since.
Look at the map, the compass, the app (GPS position without signal), the sun.
If you really don't know where you are: mark the spot (branch, coloured cloth) and explore in a star pattern, 100 steps maximum in each direction, returning to the starting point each time.
A river or a path almost always leads to houses: follow them downstream.
If night is falling or the weather is turning: settle in for the night and prepare signals rather than carrying on.
perdu_calme.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

ligne_faitiere.intro: The rope stretched between two trees is the backbone of almost every tarp shelter. Well tensioned, the tarp doesn't flap and water runs off.
etapes: Choose two healthy trees, a little further apart than the length of the tarp (4 to 5 m for a 3 m tarp).
Tie one end to the first tree with a round turn and two half hitches, at the height you want: about 1 m for a low A-frame, 1.5 m for a lean-to.
Go to the second tree, pass the rope around it and tension it with a trucker's hitch. It should ring like a guitar string.
Lock it with two slipped half hitches: you'll undo them in one pull in the morning.
Lay the tarp over the rope, or clip its eyelets on with two Prusik knots so you can slide it and tension it lengthwise.
Check that the rope is level, or slightly lower at the foot end so water runs off that way.
attention: Protect the bark with a rag or wide strap if the rope is thin, and never tighten around a young tree.
ligne_faitiere.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

goutte_eau.titre: Stopping water running into the shelter
goutte_eau.intro: In rain, water follows the ridgeline and ends up dripping… onto your sleeping bag. A simple piece of string solves the problem.
etapes: Cut two pieces of string about 20 cm long.
Tie one onto the ridgeline on each side, just before the point where the rope goes under the tarp.
Let the ends hang towards the ground: water sliding along the rope runs down the string and drips outside.
Do the same on the corner guylines if water runs along them.
If needed, dig a small channel under the edge of the tarp on the downhill side to carry away water falling from the roof.
goutte_eau.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

appentis_bache.intro: A sloping roof, open on one side only: the quickest shelter, with a nice view and room to get organised. Back to the wind.
etapes: Work out where the wind is coming from: the low side of the shelter must face it.
Rig a ridgeline about 1.2 to 1.5 m high.
Lay one edge of the tarp over the rope and tie its corners.
Pull the other edge down at a slope towards the ground, on the wind side, and peg it at ground level with pegs or sticks.
To block a side wind, fold down and peg one of the front corners, or close the side with dead branches.
Put your bedding right at the back, where the roof is lowest: that's the most sheltered area.
attention: Poorly protected if the wind changes: watch the weather and be ready to lower the front.
appentis_bache.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

soc_charrue.intro: A single high tie-out, three corners on the ground: a one-person shelter, very wind-resistant, pitched in a few minutes.
etapes: Spread the square tarp out as a diamond, one point towards the tree.
Tie that point to the tree (or to the top of a walking pole) at about 1.2 m high.
Peg the opposite point to the ground, well tensioned, on the side the wind comes from.
Peg the two side points to the ground, pulling so the fabric is taut without creases.
The opening is on the tree side, back to the wind. Slide in head towards the tree, where it's highest.
attention: Little room: ideal for a night alone, not for storing a whole pack.
soc_charrue.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

bache_tube.intro: With a big tarp, you fold the edges under you: you get a roof and a floor in one piece. Very useful when the ground is wet.
etapes: You need a tarp of at least 3 × 4 m.
Rig a low ridgeline, 80 cm to 1 m off the ground.
Drape the tarp over the rope, lengthwise.
Instead of pegging the edges, fold them inwards under the shelter: they overlap and form a floor.
Your weight on the floor tensions both sides of the roof. Weigh down the folded edges with your pack.
attention: The shelter is open at both ends: point it in the direction of the wind, never across it.
bache_tube.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

abri_poncho.intro: A rain poncho is a small tarp you wear. In an unplanned night out, it becomes a roof.
etapes: Close the hood tightly: pull the drawcord and knot it on itself so it doesn't act as a funnel.
Stretch a cord between two trees about 80 cm off the ground.
Put the poncho over it, as a lean-to or an A-frame depending on its size.
Tie the corners to pegs or roots with taut-line hitches.
Insulate the ground with your emptied pack and a thick layer of dead leaves.
abri_poncho.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

bache_tempete.titre: Pitching your tarp in rain and wind
bache_tempete.intro: In bad weather, the order of actions matters: put the roof up first, then settle underneath in the dry.
etapes: Keep the tarp and cord at the top of your pack, reachable without unpacking everything.
Rig the ridgeline first, then the tarp, before taking anything else out.
Pitch the shelter low: the lower it is, the less the wind can grab it. Edges at ground level on the wind side.
Drive the pegs in at 45°, tip towards the shelter, and double the anchors on the wind side.
Re-tension all the guylines after an hour: wet cord stretches.
Once the roof is up, set up your bedding underneath and put what must stay dry into waterproof bags.
attention: In violent wind, move away from trees: branches break and fall (see “Spotting the dangers of the camp”).
bache_tempete.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

ancrages.intro: Lost peg, ground too hard, sand or snow: there's always a way to tie down a corner of the tarp.
etapes: Wooden peg: a sound dead stick, thumb-thick, sharpened to a point, with a notch at the top for the cord. Drive it in at 45° outwards.
Stony ground: tie the cord around a big stone, or drive a peg between two stones and wedge it with a third.
Roots and stumps: simply pass the cord around them.
Sand or snow (deadman anchor): tie the cord to the middle of a stick, dig a 25 cm hole, lay the stick at the bottom across the direction of pull, fill in and pack down.
Ground too hard: put a big stone on the corner of the tarp or on a stick holding it.
ancrages.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

hamac.intro: A hammock solves the problem of wet ground, slopes and stones. But it's cold underneath and needs to be set up methodically.
etapes: Choose two healthy trees, at least as thick as a thigh, 4 to 5 m apart, with no dead branch above.
Use wide straps (at least 2.5 cm): they protect the bark. Never thin cord around a trunk.
Attach the straps at roughly eye level, so they form a 30° angle with the ground once the hammock is loaded.
Adjust the hammock so it's at chair height (45 cm) when you sit in it.
Lie diagonally: your back is almost flat and you don't feel folded in two.
Insulate underneath: under your weight, the sleeping bag compresses and no longer keeps you warm. Slip a mat into the hammock, or use an underquilt.
Stretch a tarp above, on a ridgeline higher than the straps, with drip lines on the straps.
attention: Below 10 °C, a hammock without insulation underneath is freezing, even with a good sleeping bag.
Check that trees and straps are allowed on the site.
hamac.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

abri_conique.intro: Poles stood in a cone and covered: a shelter you can sit up in, which keeps out rain well if it's steep enough.
etapes: Gather three strong dead poles about 2.5 m long.
Lash them together near one end with a tripod lashing, then spread the legs into a triangle.
Lean other poles all around, leaving a narrow opening on the side away from the wind.
Cover from the bottom up, like roof tiles, with large pieces of dead bark, dead branches, then a thick layer of leaves.
The steeper the slope, the better the water runs off: aim for really steep sides.
Insulate the ground inside with 20 to 30 cm of dry leaves.
attention: Only dead wood fallen on the ground: in Europe, cutting living branches is forbidden without the owner's permission.
Takes 2 to 4 hours: start well before nightfall, and dismantle everything when you leave.
abri_conique.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

abri_chablis.intro: The root plate of a fallen tree forms a natural wall against the wind. You can lean a lean-to against it in minutes.
etapes: First check its stability: the tree must be lying firmly on the ground, not held up by other trees.
Settle on the side sheltered from the wind, against the root plate or along the trunk.
Lean dead poles from the trunk to the ground to form a lean-to roof.
Cover with dead branches and leaves, or stretch your tarp over it.
Insulate the ground: the hollow left by the roots is often damp, fill it with dry leaves.
attention: Never cut a root of a half-uprooted tree: the root plate can spring back up suddenly and crush whatever is underneath.
The root hole fills with water in the rain: don't sleep at the bottom.
abri_chablis.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

abri_rocher.intro: An overhanging rock offers a ready-made roof. But you must check it's not dangerous.
etapes: Look at the ground: fresh rock chips or recently fallen stones point to rockfall. Move on.
Look at the ceiling: no open cracks or blocks that look loose.
Check that no water runs or drips from the rock, and that the floor isn't a temporary stream bed.
Look for animal signs (droppings, hair, bones): the place may already be occupied.
Close off the front with your tarp or dead branches to cut the wind, and insulate the ground well, which is often cold.
attention: Never light a fire right under the rock: the heat can make the stone burst and loosen slabs.
The limestone cliffs of the Ourthe are often protected sites: check that bivouacking is allowed there.
abri_rocher.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

abri_neige.intro: Snow insulates surprisingly well: a well-made shelter stays around 0 °C even when it's freezing hard outside.
etapes: At the foot of a big spruce, the low branches often form a snow-free hollow: clear it further by hand and settle underneath.
On flat ground, dig a trench as long as your body, shoulder-wide, about 1 m deep.
Cover it with dead poles or walking poles, then your tarp, then a layer of snow.
Keep a small opening, preferably lower than where you sleep: cold air stays at the bottom.
Insulate yourself from the snow underneath: mat, pack, dead branches. That's the most important thing.
Poke a ventilation hole in the roof with a stick, and check it stays open.
attention: Never a stove or candle in a poorly ventilated snow shelter: risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.
At the foot of a tree, the snow on the branches can fall in one block: don't settle there in a thaw or in wind.
abri_neige.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

dangers_camp.titre: Spotting the dangers of the camp
dangers_camp.intro: Before putting down your pack, take two minutes to look up, around and down. Most bivouac accidents come from there.
etapes: Up: look for dead branches and dead or leaning trees. Foresters call them “widowmakers”. Never sleep under them, even in calm weather.
Around: avoid ant hills, wasp nests, burrows and animal paths (narrow trails, flattened grass, wild boar rooting).
Down: no dry stream bed, hollow where water collects or low bank. A river can rise a metre overnight after a storm upstream.
Cold: cold air flows down and collects at the bottom of valleys and hollows. Settle a little above the bottom, on a ledge.
Wind: avoid summits and ridges. A forest edge or a copse cuts the wind.
Thunderstorms: no isolated tree, summit, pylon or metal fence. In a forest, a stand of trees of the same height is better.
dangers_camp.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

plan_camp.intro: A tidy camp means fewer things lost in the dark, fewer animal visits and a safer night.
etapes: Pitch the shelter first, in the best spot, back to the prevailing wind.
Kitchen area: downwind of the shelter, at least a few metres away, so smoke, sparks and smells drift away from your bed.
Water: fill your bottles before night. Wash up away from the stream (at least 60 m) and scatter the dirty water.
Toilet: at least 60 m from water, camp and paths, in a 15 cm hole filled back in.
Food: never in the shelter. Store it away from camp (see “Protecting your food from animals”).
Keep within reach at night: head torch, water, knife, whistle, phone, glasses. Always in the same place.
Before dark, walk round the camp: everything that must stay dry is put away, the wood is under the tarp, the guylines are visible (a bit of light-coloured cloth on them stops you tripping).
plan_camp.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska

nourriture_animaux.intro: In Europe, no bears, but foxes, wild boar, martens and above all rodents that can chew through a bag in one night.
etapes: Store all food and rubbish in a closed bag, odour-proof if possible (double freezer bag).
Never food in the shelter or tent: a wild boar or fox will come looking for it there.
Hang the bag from a branch at least 2 m off the ground and 1 m from the trunk, about twenty metres from where you sleep.
To hang it: tie a stone to a cord, throw it over the branch, attach the bag and hoist it up, then tie the other end to a nearby tree.
Also put toothpaste, creams and anything scented in the bag.
Never feed animals and pick up all leftovers: an animal that gets used to it becomes a problem for the next campers.
nourriture_animaux.source: Standard bivouac know-how and manuals FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain), written for Bivaska
